questions.q: Which subroutine is the entry point of a Jack program?
choices: The first function declared in the first .jack file compiled
Any function named main, in whichever class declares it
questions.explain: A Jack program is one or more classes, one of which must be named Main. Main must have a function named main, and execution begins at Main.main.

questions.q: A Jack class named Foo must be stored in its own file named Foo.jack.
questions.explain: The class is the basic compilation unit, and each class Foo lives in a separate Foo.jack file.

questions.q: Which of the following are legal Jack identifiers?
questions.explain: Identifiers are any-length sequences of letters, digits and '_', and the first character must be a letter or '_'. '2x' starts with a digit, and 'my-var' contains '-', which is the minus operator.

questions.q: How does Jack treat `-13` in source code?
choices: As an expression: the unary minus operator applied to the integer constant 13
As a syntax error, since Jack has no negative numbers
questions.explain: Integer constants range from 0 to 32767. A negative value like -13 isn't a constant. It's an expression that applies unary minus to the constant 13.

questions.q: What is the largest integer constant you can write in Jack source code?
questions.explain: Jack integer constants are values in the range 0 to 32767.

questions.q: A Jack string constant can contain any character except two. Which two are they, and how do you get them?
choices: Newline and double quote. Call String.newLine() and String.doubleQuote().
Backslash and single quote. Jack supports C-style escape sequences for them.
Tab and newline. Use the escape sequences for tab and newline.
Double quote and semicolon. Call String.doubleQuote() and String.semicolon().
questions.explain: String constants are enclosed in double quotes and can't contain a newline or a double quote. The OS functions String.newLine() and String.doubleQuote() supply those characters.

questions.q: What is the `/** ... */` comment form intended for?
choices: Comments that run to the end of the line
Disabling code during debugging; it can't hold prose
questions.explain: Jack supports three comment forms: `//` runs to the end of the line, `/* ... */` runs until the closing `*/`, and `/** ... */` is for API documentation. The compiler ignores all of them, along with white space.

questions.q: Jack is case sensitive, so `count` and `Count` are different identifiers.
questions.explain: The language is case sensitive: x and X are treated as different identifiers.

questions.q: Which Jack symbol is both the assignment operator and the equality comparison operator?
questions.explain: Jack uses a single `=` for both, e.g. `let x = 0;` and `while (~(current = null))`. There is no `==` operator.

questions.q: Which of these are primitive types in Jack?
questions.explain: Jack's primitive types are int, char and boolean. String and Array are class types from the standard library (the OS), and Jack has no floating-point type.

questions.q: Which kind of Jack variable has exactly one copy, shared by all instances of the class?
questions.explain: Only one copy of each static variable exists, and every object of the class shares it (like a private static variable in Java). Each object gets its own copy of the field variables.

questions.q: What is the scope of a field variable?
choices: The class it is declared in, except in functions, where it is undefined
Only the constructor that initializes it
The class it is declared in, including its functions
questions.explain: Fields belong to individual objects. A function operates on no particular object, so there is no current object whose fields it could use.

questions.q: You declared `var char c;` and want c to hold the character 'A'. Which statement works in Jack?
questions.explain: Jack has no character literals, so `let c = 'A';` isn't supported. Characters and integers convert freely, and 65 is the code for 'A'. A workaround is `let s = "A"; let c = s.charAt(0);`. Assigning "A" directly would store a String object's address, not the character code.

questions.q: After `var Array arr; let arr = 5000; let arr[100] = 17;` runs, which RAM address holds 17?
questions.explain: An integer assigned to a reference variable is treated as a memory address. arr[100] is the word at arr + 100, which is RAM[5100].

questions.q: Point has two int fields, x and y, and a print method that prints "(x,y)". What does this code print? `let arr = Array.new(2); let arr[0] = 2; let arr[1] = 5; let p = arr; do p.print();` (p is declared as a Point)
choices: Nothing; it's a compile-time type error
questions.explain: Jack is weakly typed, so an object can be converted into an array and back. p now points to the memory block holding [2,5], and Point's print method reads those two words as x = 2, y = 5.

questions.q: Using the Hack character set, what value does c hold after `let s = "ABC"; let c = s.charAt(1);`?
questions.explain: charAt is zero-based, so index 1 is 'B'. In the Hack character set A = 65, B = 66, C = 67.

questions.q: How do you represent a two-dimensional array in Jack?
choices: Create an array whose elements are arrays
You can't; Jack has no way to represent 2D data
questions.explain: Array.new takes a single size. To get a multi-dimensional array, create an array of arrays.

questions.q: Jack arrays are typed: an Array that holds integers can't also hold a Point or a String.
questions.explain: Jack arrays are untyped instances of the OS class Array. The lecture's example puts 12, false, a Point and a String into one 4-element array.

questions.q: What does the declaration `var String s;` create?
choices: An object variable (a pointer). The String itself still has to be created, e.g. with String.new or a string constant.
A String object with room for 0 characters
A String initialized to the empty string
questions.explain: Declaring a class-type variable only creates a reference. `var char c;`, by contrast, creates a primitive variable.

questions.q: What is the `do` statement for?
choices: Calling a function or method for its effect, ignoring any returned value
Assigning the result of a call to a variable
questions.explain: `do` must precede a function or method call made outside an expression, e.g. `do Output.println();`. Assignments use `let`.

questions.q: In Jack, you can leave out the curly braces around an if or while body when the body is a single statement.
questions.explain: The braces are mandatory even for a single statement, e.g. `if (a > 0) { return a; } else { return -a; }`.

questions.q: What is the value of the Jack expression `2 + 3 * 4`?
choices: Unpredictable, because Jack has no operator priority. Write `2 + (3 * 4)` instead.
20, since Jack evaluates strictly left to right by definition
questions.explain: Jack defines no operator priority, so the lecture calls this expression's value unpredictable. Use parentheses to enforce the order you want.

questions.q: What does the unary operator `~` do in Jack?
questions.explain: Jack has two unary operators: `-` for arithmetic negation and `~` for boolean negation, which is bit-wise for integers. For example, `~(current = null)` means current is not null.

questions.q: You can use the `this` keyword inside a function.
questions.explain: `this` denotes the current object. A function is a static method that operates on no particular object, so `this` can't be used there.

questions.q: Which of the following can be a Jack expression?
choices: A call to a subroutine whose return type is void
~done, where done is a boolean variable
questions.explain: An expression can be a constant, a variable in scope, `this` (outside functions), an array element, a call to a subroutine that returns a non-void type, a unary `-` or `~` applied to an expression, a binary operation, or a parenthesized expression. Jack has no `++` operator.

questions.q: Which of these is a legal Jack assignment to the local variable x?
questions.explain: Every assignment must start with `let`. `var` only declares locals, with a type: `var int x;`.

questions.q: How must the method `method void draw()` end?
choices: No return is needed; it can just reach the closing brace
questions.explain: Every subroutine must end with `return value;` or `return;`. Void functions and methods use `return;`, and constructors must end with `return this;`.

questions.q: Rules like requiring `let` before assignments, `do` before standalone calls, and braces around every block make Jack programs a bit harder to write but make the Jack compiler much easier to write.
questions.explain: The lecture says some of these peculiar syntax features make writing Jack programs a bit harder and writing a Jack compiler much easier.

questions.q: Which kind of Jack subroutine is a static method that operates on no particular object?
questions.explain: Constructors create new objects, methods operate on the current object, and functions are static methods that operate on no particular object.

questions.q: Inside a method of class Point, how can you read the x field of a different Point object named other?
choices: Call an accessor such as other.getx(), because all fields are private
Write this.x, which refers to other
questions.explain: In Jack all fields are private and all methods are public. You read the current object's field by just writing x (the same as this.x). For another object, you need a get/set method.

questions.q: Inside a constructor, what does `this` contain?
choices: The base address of the object the constructor created
The number of objects created so far
questions.explain: The compiled constructor calls an OS function to allocate a memory block for the new object, then sets a local `this` to the block's base address. `return this;` hands that address back to the caller.

questions.q: On the Hack platform, where do Jack objects and arrays live?
choices: On the heap, starting at RAM address 2048
On the stack, at RAM 256 to 2047
In the static variable area, starting at RAM address 16
questions.explain: Static variables start at RAM 16. The stack (256 to 2047) holds the local and argument variables of running subroutines. Objects and arrays live on the heap, which starts at 2048. A client variable like p1 sits on the stack and holds a heap address.

questions.q: In the Point class, the constructor increments the static pointCount, and plus returns Point.new(...). What number does this code print? `let p1 = Point.new(1,2); let p2 = Point.new(3,4); let p3 = p1.plus(p2); do Output.printInt(Point.getPointCount());`
questions.explain: plus creates its result by calling Point.new, so the constructor runs three times: for p1, for p2, and inside plus for p3.

questions.q: Jack has automatic garbage collection, so objects you no longer need are reclaimed for you.
questions.explain: Jack has no garbage collection. Best practice is to dispose an object once you no longer need it, and to give every class that has constructors a dispose method that calls Memory.deAlloc(this).

questions.q: Inside method f of class Foo, what does `do g();` do?
choices: Calls method g of class Foo on the current (this) object
Calls function g of class Foo with no object
Nothing; it's illegal because every call must name a class or object
questions.explain: An unqualified call means a method of the current class, called on `this`. That's why it can't appear inside a function. Calling a function requires the class name, e.g. `do Foo.p(3);`.

questions.q: Every Jack class must declare at least one constructor.
questions.explain: A Jack class has 0 or more constructors, one of which is normally named new. A class like Main, which only has the function main, needs none.

questions.q: What makes up a Jack class declaration?
choices: Field variable declarations, static variable declarations, and subroutine declarations
Import statements, field declarations, and method declarations
Local variable declarations, statements, and a return
An interface, a constructor, and a destructor
questions.explain: A class is a sequence of field declarations, static variable declarations, and subroutine declarations (constructors, methods and functions).

questions.q: How does the lecture define a list recursively?
choices: Either null, or a value followed by a list
An array whose last element is null
questions.explain: A list is the value null, or a value followed by a list. So (3, 5, 2) is (3, (5, (2, null))). The List class mirrors this with an int field `data` and a List field `next`.

questions.q: What does `do v.print();` display after `let v = List.new(2, null); let v = List.new(5, v); let v = List.new(3, v);`?
questions.explain: Each List.new(car, cdr) makes a new node whose next field points at the existing list, so the node created last becomes the head. The result is the list (3, 5, 2).

questions.q: In `constructor List new(int car, List cdr)`, what does `let next = cdr;` do?
choices: Links the new node to the list that was passed in
Advances an iterator to the next node
questions.explain: The constructor stores car in data, stores the reference cdr in next (no copying), then returns this. The new node is now the head of the old list.

questions.q: List.print starts with `let current = this;` and loops `while (~(current = null)) { ...; let current = current.getNext(); }`. When does the loop stop?
choices: After the last node is printed, when current becomes null
Immediately, because current starts as null
Never, unless the body executes an explicit return
questions.explain: current starts at the first node. Each pass prints current's data and moves to the next node. The last node's next is null, so the condition fails after that node is printed.

questions.q: List.dispose runs `if (~(next = null)) { do next.dispose(); }` and then `do Memory.deAlloc(this);`. For the list (3, 5, 2), in what order are the nodes freed?
choices: All three at the same moment
Only 3 is freed; the other nodes leak
questions.explain: Each call disposes its tail before freeing itself. The recursion reaches node 2, whose next is null, so node 2 is freed first. Then the call on 5 resumes and frees 5, and finally the call on 3 frees 3.

questions.q: The client calls v.dispose() on a 3-element list. Counting that call, how many times does dispose() run in total?
questions.explain: dispose runs once per node: the client's call on the head, plus one recursive next.dispose() call for each of the two remaining nodes.

questions.q: When v.dispose() starts executing, what is `this` set to?
choices: The object dispose was called on (the node v points to)
The last node of the list
questions.explain: The compiled method creates a local variable named this and sets it to the object the method was called on. In the recursive call next.dispose(), this is the next node.

questions.q: What best practice does the lecture recommend for code that builds and manipulates lists?
choices: Move it from the client into the List class, e.g. an append method or a constructor that takes an array
Keep it in Main so the List class stays small
Store the list's head and tail in static variables
Skip constructors and build nodes with Memory.alloc
questions.explain: Building a list by chaining List.new calls in client code works, but the lecture says there are better and safer ways and that construction/manipulation code belongs in the List class.

questions.q: Which of the following are classes in the Jack OS?
questions.explain: The Jack OS classes are Math, String, Array, Output, Screen, Keyboard, Memory and Sys. It has no File or Thread classes.

questions.q: What does `do Memory.poke(513, Memory.peek(512));` do?
choices: Sets RAM[513] to the value of RAM[512]
Sets RAM[512] to the value of RAM[513]
questions.explain: Memory.peek(address) returns the value stored at that address, and Memory.poke(address, value) writes value there.

questions.q: What does this code display? `do Output.printInt(97); do Output.printChar(97); do Output.printString("a");`
questions.explain: printInt prints the number 97. printChar prints the character whose code is 97, which is 'a'. printString prints the string "a".

questions.q: How is the screen laid out for text written with the Output class?
questions.explain: Output treats the screen as 23 rows of 64 characters, black and white, in a fixed font defined in the Output class.

questions.q: What is the resolution of the screen that the Screen class draws on?
choices: 256 rows of 512 pixels, black and white
480 rows of 640 pixels, black and white
questions.explain: The Hack screen is 256 rows by 512 pixels, black and white. Screen offers clearScreen, setColor, drawPixel, drawLine, drawRectangle and drawCircle.

questions.q: How long does `do Sys.wait(1000);` pause?
choices: One second (the duration is in milliseconds)
questions.explain: Sys.wait takes a duration in milliseconds. Sys also provides halt() and error(errorCode).

questions.q: How does the lecture describe a language's standard class library?
choices: As a language-specific OS that closes gaps between high-level programs and the hardware
As an optional add-on that most programs avoid
As the part of the compiler that parses expressions
As a replacement for the VM
questions.explain: Most languages are simple, and their power comes from an open-ended standard class library. The Jack OS is that library for Jack: it closes gaps between programs and the host hardware and provides efficient implementations of common functions and ADTs.

questions.q: Which expression gets the last character of the String str?
questions.explain: Characters are indexed from 0 to length() - 1 and read with the String method charAt. String has no lastChar method, and a String is an object, not an Array, so you can't index it with brackets.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a function in the Jack OS Math class?
questions.explain: Math provides abs, multiply, divide, min, max and sqrt. It has no pow.

questions.q: Square Dance is built from three classes. Which one creates a Square and runs the loop that reads keys and moves, resizes, or quits?
questions.explain: Square represents a graphical square object. SquareGame creates a Square and loops over the user's input. Main creates a SquareGame, runs it, and then disposes it.

questions.q: SquareGame.run first loops `while (key = 0) { let key = Keyboard.keyPressed(); do moveSquare(); }`, handles the key, and then loops `while (~(key = 0)) { let key = Keyboard.keyPressed(); do moveSquare(); }`. What does the second loop do?
choices: Waits for the key to be released while keeping the square moving
Waits for a key to be pressed
Deletes the typed characters from the keyboard buffer
questions.explain: The first loop waits for a key press and the second waits for its release. Both call moveSquare, so the square keeps moving in its current direction. This is the typical way interactive Jack apps handle keyboard events.

questions.q: In the Hack character set, what code does Keyboard.keyPressed() return for the up-arrow key?
questions.explain: The arrow keys are left 130, up 131, right 132 and down 133. Newline is 128. SquareGame sets direction = 1 (up) when key = 131.

questions.q: Why does Square.moveUp redraw only two rows instead of erasing and redrawing the whole square?
choices: Moving up 2 pixels changes only the bottom two rows (which become background) and the top two rows (which become black), so updating just those is cheaper
Screen.drawRectangle can draw at most two rows at a time
The square is only two pixels tall
To create a deliberate flicker effect
questions.explain: moveUp calls setColor(false) to erase the bottom two rows, subtracts 2 from y, then calls setColor(true) to draw the two new top rows. Every other pixel stays black.

questions.q: Drawing a 16x16 sprite with Screen.drawPixel took 75 drawing operations. How many Memory.poke writes does the optimized version need?
questions.explain: Each 16-pixel row of the sprite fits in one 16-bit word of the screen memory map, so one poke per row draws the whole sprite: 16 writes.

questions.q: A sprite row is 0001100000110000 in binary. What decimal value do you poke into screen memory for that row?
questions.explain: The 1 bits are worth 4096 + 2048 + 32 + 16 = 6192.

questions.q: Generated sprite code computes memAddress = 16384 + location and then pokes one word per sprite row. A screen row is 512 pixels and each memory word holds 16 pixels. How many words apart are the addresses of two vertically adjacent sprite rows?
questions.explain: One screen row takes 512 / 16 = 32 words, so the next row down starts 32 words later. That's why the generated code pokes memAddress+0, +32, +64, and so on.

questions.q: According to the lecture's best practice, when should you draw with Memory.poke instead of the Screen class?
choices: For high-performance sprites. Use Screen for simple graphics.
Never, because Jack forbids poking screen memory
questions.explain: For simple graphics, use the standard OS library (Screen). For high-performance sprites, design the image in a bitmap editor and write it straight into the screen memory map with Memory.poke.

questions.q: Jack supports inheritance between classes.
questions.explain: Jack's limitations include a primitive type system, few control structures, some peculiar syntax, and no inheritance. The goal is a minimal language that a simple compiler can implement.

questions.q: Why is Jack designed to be weakly typed with full memory access?
choices: To give the programmer full control of the platform, especially when writing the OS
To make programs run faster in the VM emulator
Because strong typing is impossible on 16-bit hardware
questions.explain: Weak typing and full memory access (e.g. casting integers to addresses, Memory.peek/poke) give the programmer full control of the computer, which matters most when writing the OS.
